Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era.
Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO, Colette Kress, has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’ public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s money-hungry workforce . And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ’24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.”
By WIRED’s count, Kress has publicly used the phrase three times in the past 24 hours, often putting emphasis or a little bit of zhuzh in it:
“Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.”
“Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change. We thank you all for the great quarter that we had. Just remember, we’ve got this.”
Kress ended Wednesday’s meeting by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game, all singing together.
“It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. But Nvidia, we’ve got this.”
Kress’ new catchphrase perhaps isn’t the most inspiring; companies that got this usually don’t have to remind people how much they got this twice in one meeting. It’s a collectivist’s version of “You got this,” a slightly less corny version of “Yes we can,” a saying that may well pose more questions than it answers. (We got … what?)
Nvidia investors, or any investor, might not have fist-pumped and said “We’ve got this!” during a quick portfolio check these past 10 days. Anyone who has had the slightest hint of knowledge that Nvidia’s chips were finding their way into China is unlikely to be in a “We totally got this” mood at the moment.
Still, some Nvidia employees appear to be inspired by Kress’ mantra. “Damn right we got this,” Aaron Erickson, Nvidia’s head of NemoClaw engineering, posted on X on Wednesday. Vega Shah, who works in portfolio management for Nvidia’s venture capital arm, shared Erickson’s post and echoed the phrase , adding her own rocket ship emoji to the post.
And yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite some calls on social media and within the company to put Huang back in the top spot.

After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models.
Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the company’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Whether investors agree will become apparent on midday Thursday when Anthropic shares begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.
The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models.
“The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” says Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?”
Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth.
The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the company held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates.
Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since .
For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures , shifting priorities , and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks.
Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring , while operating losses are declining . Its big spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” says Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures.
Because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money.
The IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.)
Anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of new regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries .
Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate new types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives.
Some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing a belief that humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without even more focus on keeping models under human control. But, more recently, Coxon was quoted by the Stanford Daily as saying that he might return to Anthropic because he suspects he could have “more of an impact” working on safety there.
Notably, Amodei mentioned safety as a challenge even above access to electricity for data centers, which many other AI companies list as their top issue. On the ground, people opposing data centers have griped about not just higher power bills, but also construction-induced traffic and housing woes, environmental pollution, and a lack of significant financial benefit.
At data center developer Nscale’s site for Anthropic in West Virginia, extreme rain combined with grading (leveling or sloping ground for construction) coincided with flooding in neighbor’s backyards. “We’re frustrated, we’re angry,” the community spokesperson Matheny says. “We want [data centers] in more logical locations and not to be considering profit as the only guideline.” (Nscale says it has fixed damage and bought out some homeowners at above-market rates.)
Environmental activists have pointed out that Anthropic has made no commitment about using renewable power at its data centers, and has never published an environmental impact report.
“Clearly permitting a new data center development will be extremely difficult in the US,” Tunguz says. Pushback could force Anthropic and others to focus outside the US for data centers. That will add risk, complexity, and cost, he says.
A handful of labor groups and others including National Nurses United urged retirement funds to steer clear of the IPO, saying they “should not be invested in companies that harm our communities and allow a handful of individuals to accumulate historic fortunes and power.”
Yolanda Daniel, a member of the homeowner associations’ coalition Environmental Advocates Mississippi, says Anthropic is socializing the cost of AI development and privatizing the gains from it. “That is not how a public benefit corporation operates,” she says, vowing to do everything she can to stop next year’s planned opening of an Anthropic data center across the street from her.
Anthropic’s IPO paperwork argued some of its public benefit will materialize as employees and early investors become some of the world’s biggest philanthropists . But there’s no guarantee of that, or that anyone will give away their money to causes that directly benefit disgruntled communities. And if employees donate shares to one of the philanthropic funds the company offers, they also consolidate power with Amodei by handing over their voting rights to him.
Amodei and his fellow cofounders collectively hold a majority of Anthropic’s shareholder voting power. Some investor watchdogs have warned about what they view as concentrated control . But a successful debut will show investor…

What studying the ketogenic diet for eating disorder patients tells us about the future of mental health research in the US.
In a dark room, a man with a camera makes his pitch: Therapy isn’t the first treatment you should get if you have anorexia or bulimia, he says. He’s in his late 20s, wearing a backward camo baseball cap and a silver chain. “Instead of going straight to the therapy, let’s do a keto diet where we encourage you to eat as much as you want” — all while limiting your carbohydrate intake to 30 grams a day. He tells his viewers that this shift will force your brain to use a different fuel source, and “all those defective neural pathways that were causing you to engage in that eating disorder, they heal up and they start to work correctly.”
“Suddenly, that eating disorder is not there anymore,” he says.
There is no evidence to support the man’s claim. In fact, most of the psychiatrists and nutritionists The Verge spoke with for this story said that treating an eating disorder with a restrictive diet is just too risky.
“This intervention right now would be reasonably viewed as dangerous or high risk,” says Kylie Jeffrey, a nutrition scientist at Duke University. “I think that’s a danger,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist and the founding director of the University of North Carolina’s Center of Excellence for Eating Disorders. “Don’t try this at home.”
National Alliance for Eating Disorders helpline : Call 1-866-662-1235 for help finding treatment options at all levels of care, or check the alliance’s national database for treatment options.
ANAD helpline : Call 1-888-375-7767 for emotional support and treatment referrals.
Crisis Text Line : Text HOME to 741-741 from anywhere in the US, at any time, about any type of crisis.
988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline : Call or text 988 (formerly known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline). The original phone number, 1-800-273-TALK (8255), is available as well.
Befrienders Worldwide has a network of crisis helplines active in 48 countries. Click here to find them .
As with many spurious health claims, this one didn’t come out of nowhere. The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, very low-carb diet that can cause people to go into “ketosis,” a state in which a person’s cells begin to burn fat, in the form of ketone bodies, instead of sugar. And researchers have started to study its use to treat anorexia nervosa. But because the research has barely begun, no one knows if this will work. And although some researchers think that trying to treat a disease involving food restriction with a limited diet might be dangerous, others are excited about the possibility of new treatments. They just want to see data from large, rigorous clinical trials to make sure that keto actually is a treatment.
On the internet, however, the ketogenic diet is already being promoted as an “effective” way to treat eating disorders. The man in the camo hat — his name is Matthew — is an important part of how that message has spread. Matthew’s audience is small. He has a few thousand followers on YouTube and Instagram. And the video in which he talks about eating disorders going away on keto has a little under 1,000 views on YouTube at the time of reporting. But it would be a mistake to evaluate his reach and influence solely based on his view counts. Because in the “Make America Healthy Again”-coded world of ketogenic diet influencers, Matthew is about as connected as it gets.
Matthew’s father is David Baszucki, the CEO and cofounder of the gaming platform Roblox. It’s the largest gaming platform in the world, with more than 100 million daily active users, most of them kids and teens (though there are plenty of adults, too). Thanks to Roblox, his net worth sits somewhere between $3 billion and $5 billion . And since 2021, David and his wife Jan Ellison Baszucki have put more than $105 million toward funding research , clinical care , and advocacy work that revolves around metabolic health, with more than $55 million dedicated to the use of a ketogenic diet to treat mental illness. They’re considered big players in this burgeoning space.
I first heard about the Baszuckis’ philanthropic interests in December 2025, when a podcast producer emailed me to ask if I would be interested in hosting a new show funded by a nonprofit organization. Over the phone, I learned that the podcast would mainly be covering a new study by a researcher named Guido Frank in which scientists had investigated the use of the ketogenic diet to treat anorexia nervosa. I also learned that the nonprofit that had funded the study, Baszucki Group, would also be funding the podcast. I declined to participate in the project.
The Baszuckis feel strongly about the impact of their philanthropy. “Baszucki Group has been the catalyst for a growing body of research targeting metabolic root causes of mental illness with therapeutic ketogenic interventions,” Baszucki Group spokesperson Maura Siefring wrote in an email to The Verge .
Matthew’s own compelling story is what got his parents interested in this kind of philanthropy — though that story has never included an eating disorder. “I healed my own bipolar disorder using a ketogenic diet,” Matthew says in many of his videos. “And now I’m on a mission to help other people recover.” Keto is a specific area of interest for Matthew, who highlighted his parents’ role in funding this research in a June video called “This Keto Anorexia Study Just Broke the Internet.”
“Broke the internet” is something of an overstatement. Still, Dr. Guido Frank, a psychiatrist at the University of California, San Diego, and the lead author of the trial, published in Communications Medicine , tells The Verge , “I am extremely hopeful that this could be — this is a little bit dramatic, but a game-changing intervention … I haven’t seen such good results throughout my whole career.”
In the small, 14-week study, which Frank’s team conducted with a $235,000 donation from the Baszuckis, researchers recruited 22 people who were either slightly underweight or weight “normalized,” meaning that they were neither overweight nor underweight. The goal was to see if it was safe and feasible to use the ketogenic diet as an anorexia treatment. Of the 18 people who completed the study, “none of them lost weight,” Frank says. But what’s remarkable, he says, is that 12 of those 18 participants experienced a decrease in their eating disorder and depression symptoms, such that they no longer met the diagnostic criteria for anorexia nervosa. “This is not something that you typically see in the other available treatments that we have.”
The study didn’t require that participants receive any form of therapy during the trial period, and if you asked Matthew, he might tell you that’s a good thing. His videos frequently proclaim the dangers of conventional psychiatric treatments. “There’s a malicious force trying to cripple us, trying to feed us this snake oil,” he says in a video posted in March. That seems to be a common refrain among ketogenic diet influencers.
“There are a lot of people who are going to use metabolic psychiatry and the ketogenic diet to disparage psychiatry in a way that’s wholly inappropriate,” says Dr. Drew Ramsey, a nutritional psychiatrist. “And that’s not helpful to patients and families because there are lots of people out there currently in full remission from their mental illness with the treatments that we have,” including therapy and medications — “millions and millions of people.”

But that statistic hides an important fact about the kind of research that the federal government funds. The Voyager 1 spacecraft launched from Earth in September 1977.
It’s not just old; it’s also really far away. In fact, it’s so far that it takes light one whole day to travel from the spacecraft to Earth and vice versa. That puts its distance at one light-day.
The expanse separating it from Earth raises so many interesting physics questions about Voyager 1’s epic, well, voyage . Let’s get to the questions—and the answers.
In science, we like to measure things, including distance. Surely, you’re familiar with meters. If you put a mass on a string and let it swing back and forth (like the pendulum of a clock), it will take about 1 second to go from side to side if the string is 1 meter long.
But if you want to measure larger distances like the proximity of stuff in space, this unit quickly becomes silly because objects are so far apart. While kilometers can be helpful for measuring the distance between things like Earth and the International Space Station or the moon, even they become hard to comprehend at larger scales.
Enter the Astronomical Unit , or AU, which is the average distance from the sun to the Earth, or about 1.5 x 10 11 meters. Humans found this distance by observing the transit of Venus. This transit is like a solar eclipse, except instead of the moon passing in front of the sun, it’s the planet Venus. Looking at Venus’ movement from different locations on Earth, the planet creates a shadow at different times. If you know the radius of the Earth, you can find this distance from the Earth to sun.
But what if you want to measure the distance to a star outside the solar system? AUs start to become a little unwieldy. Enter the parsec. No matter what Han Solo says in Star Wars , the parsec is a unit of distance and not the best time for the Kessel Run .
And it’s a long distance: for comparison, 1 parsec is about 200,000 AUs. The parsec is a way to measure distance using parallax. You can get the mechanics of parallax by holding your thumb out with an extended arm in front of your face. Close one eye and line up your thumb with an object across the room. Now close that eye and open your other eye. You will notice that the thumb seems to shift its position. The size of the angular shift depends on both the distance between observation locations—the distance between your eyes—and the distance to the object. The farther the object, the less parallax shift you will observe.
As Earth orbits the sun, we have different observation locations while looking at stars. Imagine an observation shift of 1 AU (you would get a 2 AU shift going from December to June). If a star has a parallax shift of 1 arc-second, we say it has a distance of 1 parsec.
At one point, astronomer Friedrich Bessel was using parallax to measure the distance to a star. He said that it was so far away that it would take light 10.3 years to reach the Earth. Boom, there’s your unit of distance, the light-year. It’s the distance light travels in one year, or 9.9 x 10 15 meters, or over 6 million AU. But we can use any unit of time to measure distance with light. One light-day is the distance that light travels in 24 hours, or 2.6 x 10 13 meters. That’s really far. In fact, no human-made object has gone farther. Let’s say that Voyager traveled at a constant speed and in a straight line (it didn’t). That would give it an average speed of 164 kilometers per second or about 36,000 mph.
Voyager has felt a lot of different forces out in space. The first is the rockets that got it there. But let’s talk about the other ones it has encountered.
First, there’s gravitational force. There is an attractive gravitational force between any two objects with mass. The force depends on the masses of the two objects and the distance between them. The force is there on any number of scales: Since your body has a mass (maybe around 70 kilograms) and your phone has a mass (about 200 grams), there is an attractive force. If the phone is about 50 centimeters from your body, the gravitational force the phone exerts on you is about 4 x 10 -9 newtons. In other words, it’s exceedingly tiny. (Depending on how much you love your phone, though, the attraction may feel stronger.)
For Voyager, there’s also a gravitational interaction with masses—like the outer planets it was originally launched to observe, as well as Earth. However, the really big gravitational influence is from the sun, since it has such a large mass (2 x 10 30 kilograms). Using the mass of Voyager 1 at 722 kilograms, there is an attractive force of 1.4 x 10 -4 newtons. That’s equivalent to the weight of 78 grains of salt on the surface of the Earth.
The only other object that would have a substantial relationship to Voyager 1 is the planet Jupiter, with a mass of 1.9 x 10 27 kilograms. But it’s only when Voyager was fairly close to the planet way back in 1979 that this gravitational force would even partially compare to the interaction with the sun.
There are other, more exotic interactions with the spacecraft, but these forces are also tiny. Solar winds—charged particles emitted from the surface of the sun—have blown past Voyager. Although they travel very fast, the mass of these particles is extremely small. The further you get from the sun, the more their intensity decreases as well.
The venerable craft is also likely to feel the impacts of magnetic fields and other weird things as it moves from a region where the primary interactions are with the sun—the heliosphere—to interactions with other stars and stuff—the interstellar medium.
Newton’s second law of motion says that forces on an object change its motion. As an equation, we can write this as net force = mass times acceleration. The acceleration is defined as the time rate of change of the velocity.
Let’s take the average speed we calculated above of 164 kilometers per second for simplicity’s sake. Does this velocity change? Yes. Remember, we calculated the gravitational force from the sun with a value of 1.4 x 10 -4 newtons. To further simplify things, let’s assume that’s the only force acting on Voyager. Using that and the mass of the spacecraft, we get an acceleration of around 2 x 10 -7 newtons. Since the gravitational force is mostly in the opposite direction as the motion of the spacecraft, though, this translates to a very slight deceleration . In one day of travel, Voyager 1 will only slow down by 0.012 meters per second.
Not much on a daily basis, but the craft does indeed slow down. Will this eventually make it stop? Actually, no. Remember, Voyager is moving away from the sun. That means that while it slows down a bit every day, it’s also getting farther from the sun and its gravitational force—the very thing slowing it down in the first place.
It’s possible for an object to always slow down but never stop, and it will “escape” from the sun. Perhaps it’s not surprising that we call this the escape velocity. For the location of the Voyager, it needs to have a speed of at least 3.2 kilometers per second. If Voyager were slower, it would essentially “fall” back to the sun, just like an apple tossed in the air falls back to the Earth.
Of course, there are always things out there that could unexpectedly impact Voyager 1. Even a very tiny amount of interstellar dust will eventually slow it down further and perhaps even stop it. Or who knows, maybe it will become self-aware and turn into the V’Ger from Star Trek: The Motion Picture . Only time will tell.

Maybe I'm just a hermit (or maybe everything in NYC is too damned expensive), but some of the most fun I've had in recent memory hasn't been going out. It's been in homes, whether it's for family movie night or for catching up with friends over drinks.
Upgrading your home entertainment setup is more than just buying a new TV or projector. Pair it with a new espresso machine or pizza oven, and you'll have the recipe for a go-to hosting location for get-togethers of all types. Below are some of the best pieces of WIRED-tested gear to upgrade any home entertainment setup, for yourself or for someone who would be over the moon unboxing a new set of speakers.
Looking for more gifting inspiration? Check out our guides to the Best Gifts for Mom , Best Gifts for Friends , Best Techie Gifts , and Best Gifts for Outdoorsy Folks .
Quite simply the best OLED TV we've tested, the Samsung S95H is bright, clear, and colorful, with outstanding picture quality and AI optimizations that eke out as much detail as possible. It's also a looker, with a silver bezel around the screen that gives the illusion of a metal picture frame. It comes in sizes ranging from 55 inches to 83 inches.
It's the best soundbar you can get, as well as the best all-in-one home theater audio solution. Everything from the unboxing down to the texture of the bar itself is premium with the Sonos Arc Ultra . And most importantly, its sound is stunning, especially considering it's slim footprint.
Looking to replicate the movie-going experience? The LG Sound Suite H7 is a great soundbar that comes in plenty of bundles with other LG subwoofers and wireless speakers. My favorite is the Immersive Suite 5 Pro bundle , which comes with the soundbar, a subwoofer, and two wireless speakers.
A premium home theater projector can make movies look bigger and better than even some of the best TVs. This Leica Cine Play 1 is a perfect example. Colors pop with vivid clarity, and you can project a 65- to 300-inch image—big enough for even the largest of parties.
Bookshelf speakers have a certain je ne sais quoi about them that other speakers can only dream of. The KEF LSX II have that classy bookshelf look with seriously modern smarts inside. You can plug these into your TV, turntable, and additional subwoofers, or forego cables entirely and use them via Wi-Fi or Bluetooth.
Want a 100-inch TV that will truly impress? You need an RGB TV like the LG Micro RGB Evo above. RGB is the latest innovation to hit TV screens, with vibrant and bold colors you'd be hard-pressed to find elsewhere.
Light can add a new level of immersion to any home theater. The Nanoleaf 4D Kit did just that for WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell. “I watched Return of the King with 4D lighting, and I never want to go back.”
This weighted blanket comes recommended by WIRED reviewer Molly Higgins , and it makes any movie night instantly cozy, regardless of the weather. It's woven from 100 percent cotton and comes in four different weight options, ranging from 10 to 25 pounds.
On the opposite end of the spectrum, this fluffy, stretchy blanket is like being surrounded by a cloud, says Higgins. “I promise this gift will be fought over at the next movie night.”
Entertainment equipment doesn't have to be drab blocks of black or white. The Audioengine Color of the Year kit comes with a turntable, bookshelf speakers, and a subwoofer, all in matching bright yellow. It's a cinch to set up and a great way to add music and color to any room.
Entertainment isn't restricted to the TV room. A great turntable makes any room a space for gathering and enjoying some music. This one from Fluance is one of our favorites, with a warm, subtle design and premium components.
Pair the RT81+ turntable with a matching set of these Fluance bookshelf speakers and you've got a setup that can deliver incredible clarity for everything, including vinyl and Bluetooth streaming.
An instant camera equals instant party favors—they've certainly been used at basically every wedding I've been to recently. Whether you're hosting a monthly movie night or a big NFL watch party, this instant camera is chic and can instantly print out photos for anyone to take home.
Elegant. Precise. Beautiful. Functional. We love this electric kettle for all these reasons. Why for home entertainment? Well, a lot of people I host prefer tea to beer, especially as winter approaches.
This sleek semiautomatic espresso machine is quite showy in person. It has a dual boiler, meaning you can froth milk as you're pulling a shot, and it comes with plenty of accessories.
Want a drink with your entertainment? This toolkit elevates the mixing experience, with a diamond-cut mixing glass , julep strainer , stainless steel jigger , and stainless steel teardrop bar spoon . All pieces are made in Japan and sourced by Umami Mart, an independently owned small business in Oakland, California.
Take your movie literally anywhere with this compact portable projector. It has a built-in stand, which is also how you adjust the projector angle. The stand also makes it easy to store anywhere in the house. The battery won't last through a whole movie, so it's better for shorter TV shows or paired with a backup portable power station .
If you have an outlet outside (or a portable power station), the Nebula X1 is one of the best compact projectors for entertainment anywhere. It's bright, colorful, and displays an image up to 200 inches. Plus, you can bundle it with wireless speakers or karaoke mics .
The Sonos Move 2 is the most-used speaker in my apartment because it is so versatile. Leave it docked indoors and you have a smart, Wi-Fi connected home speaker for music. Take it outdoors, and you have a powerful, durable Bluetooth speaker with IP56 dust and water resistance. Pair two with a Sonos soundbar, and you have an impromptu surround sound experience.
An outdoor pizza oven is a show all on its own, but pair it with an outdoor projector, and you've got entertainment (and food) for everyone. The Karu 2 is the best one we've tested.
String lights aren't just for holidays anymore. Think of them more like great outdoor lights that can go anywhere: around a big tree, along a fence line, wherever.

AK Parti Samsun Milletvekili Mehmet Muş başkanlığında toplanan Komisyonda, Dışişleri Bakanlığının 2027 yılı bütçesi, kesin hesabı ve Sayıştay raporlarının yanı sıra Avrupa Birliği Başkanlığı ile Türk Akreditasyon Kurumunun bütçe, kesin hesap ve Sayıştay raporları, Avrupa Birliği Eğitim ve Gençlik Programları Merkezi Başkanlığının (Türkiye Ulusal Ajansı) Sayıştay raporu görüşülecek.

Bu yılın, belirsizliklerin arttığı, ihtilafların tek bir bölgeyle sınırlı kalmayarak küresel barış ve istikrarı tehdit ettiği bir sene olduğunu ifade eden Fidan, küresel barış ve güvenliğin sağlanması noktasında yetersiz kalan uluslararası sistemin etkinliği ve meşruiyetinin giderek daha fazla sorgulandığını belirtti.
Fidan, "10 yılı aşkın bir süreden beri Sayın Cumhurbaşkanımızın her vesileyle gündeme getirdiği reform ihtiyacı artık daha fazla kabul görmektedir. Dijital egemenlik, geleneksel egemenliğin yeni boyutlarından biri haline gelmiştir. Bu nedenle, yapay zeka başta olmak üzere yeni teknolojiler bir rekabet ve kutuplaşma alanı haline gelme riski taşımaktadır. Bunun yanı sıra, dünya ticareti açısından kritik öneme sahip uluslararası deniz yollarında giderek artan çatışmalar nedeniyle seyrüsefer güvenliği tehdit altında bulunmaktadır." değerlendirmesinde bulundu.
Hürmüz ve Babülmendep boğazlarında yıl boyunca devam eden krizler ile Karadeniz'deki çatışmaların, başta Afrika olmak üzere, kırılgan coğrafyalarda gıda ve enerji güvenliğinin karşı karşıya kaldığı risklerin giderek büyüdüğünün altını çizen Fidan, belirsizliğin temel parametre halini aldığı mevcut ortamda Türkiye'nin, yaşanan küresel sarsıntıları en yakından hisseden ülkelerden biri olduğunu aktardı.
Fidan, "Küresel rekabet sahalarının kesişim noktasında yer alan Türkiye'nin, dünyanın içinden geçmekte olduğu dönüşüm sürecini dışarıdan izleme gibi bir şansı yoktur. Belirsizlikler döneminde yürütmekte olduğumuz çok boyutlu dış politikayla hem bölgemizde hem dünya genelinde barış ve istikrarı tesis etmek için sorumluluk üstlenmekten kaçınmıyoruz." diye konuştu.
Bölge dışı aktörlerin müdahil olduğu sorunların çözüme kavuşmadığının, aksine daha da karmaşıklaştığının dünyanın farklı bölgelerindeki örneklerden görüldüğüne işaret eden Fidan, bölgenin kendi dinamiklerine dayanan yapıcı girişimlere duyulan ihtiyacın her zamankinden daha belirgin hale geldiğini anlattı.
Bakan Fidan, bu nedenle bölgesel sahiplenme ilkesini kalıcı ve sürdürülebilir işbirliği mekanizmalarının inşa edilmesi için temel bir parametre olarak değerlendirildiğini belirterek, şunları kaydetti:
"Bu anlayış doğrultusunda yürüttüğümüz dış politikayla, 2026 yılı boyunca, Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan ile, Yüce Meclisimizin 5 Kasım'da onayladığı Ortak Savunma için Mekke Anlaşması'nı imzalayarak Orta Doğu'da kapsayıcı bir bölgesel güvenlik mimarisinin temellerini attık. Mekke İttifakı'nın kurumsallaşması yönünde somut adımlarla ilerliyoruz. Aynı zamanda, bölgemizde sürdürülebilir bir işbirliği mimarisinin oluşturulması için Suudi Arabistan, Mısır ve Pakistan ile Bölgesel Dörtlü (R4) mekanizmasını teşkil ettik. Bölgesel Dörtlü'yü Avrupa'nın öndegelen dört ülkesi Birleşik Krallık, Fransa, Almanya ve İtalya'dan oluşan E4 grubuyla İstanbul'da bir araya getirerek, Avrupa ile Orta Doğu'nun bölgesel ve küresel meseleleri birlikte ele aldığı yeni bir platformun da temelini attık."
İsrail ve ABD'nin İran'a yönelik saldırılarıyla başlayan ve İran'ın bölge ülkelerini hedef almasıyla genişleyen savaşın olumsuz yansımaları karşısında reaktif değil, proaktif bir diplomasi yürütüldüğüne dikkati çeken Fidan, Türkiye'nin İslamabad Mutabakat Zaptı'na giden sürece önemli katkılar sağladığını söyledi.
Fidan, çatışmaların yeniden başlamasını önlemek amacıyla Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan öncülüğünde gayretlerin sürdürüldüğünü söyleyerek, NATO'nun geleceğini şekillendiren Ankara Zirvesi'ne ev sahipliği yapıldığını anımsattı.
Türkiye'nin katkısıyla yeni Avrupa güvenlik mimarisinin kurulmasına dair çalışmalarda öncü ve önemli bir rol üstlendiğini vurgulayan Fidan, "Ukrayna'daki savaşın sona erdirilmesi yönünde diplomasi ve diyaloğu önceleyen istikrarlı, dengeli ve gerektiğinde inisiyatif kullanmaktan çekinmeyen bir politika izledik. Diğer aktörlerin de artık diplomasi yoluyla kalıcı çözüm bulunması ihtiyacı konusunda ülkemizle aynı noktaya geldiğini gözlemliyoruz." diye konuştu.
Hakan Fidan, 2026'da, bölgesel sahiplenme ilkesi temelinde oluşturulan yapıcı ve sorumluluk sahibi dış politikanın, hem bölgede hem küresel ölçekte Türkiye'nin çekim gücünü artırdığını ifade ederek, sözlerini şöyle sürdürdü:
"Türk Dünyası ile işbirliğimizi derinleştirmeye devam ettik. Türk Devletleri Teşkilatı'nın 13. Zirvesi'ne Cumhuriyet Bayramımızda Ankara'da evsahipliği yaparak Dönem Başkanlığı'nı devraldık. Dönem Başkanlığımız sırasında Teşkilatımızın Türk Dünyası'nın temel işbirliği platformu niteliğini pekiştirmeyi hedefliyoruz. Köklü bağlara sahip olduğumuz Balkanlar'daki anlaşmazlıkların diyalog yoluyla çözümü için 2025 yılında kurduğumuz Balkan Barış Platformu'nun Üçüncü Bakanlar Toplantısı'nı nisan ayında tertipledik. Malumunuz bu toplantı da sürekli İstanbul'da oluyor. Bağlantısallıktan teknolojiye, kültürden beşeri temaslara kadar farklı alanlarda Balkanlar'daki işbirliğimizi derinleştirmeye devam ediyoruz."
Dışişleri Bakanı Fidan, 2008'den bu yana stratejik ortak olunan Afrika Birliği ile Dördüncü Ortaklık Zirvesi'nin 9 Aralık'ta Libya'da düzenleneceğini, böylece Afrika ile ilişkileri daha da güçlendirerek yeni bir dönemin başlatılmasının hedeflendiğini belirtti.
"Küresel önemi artan Asya'daki etkimizi de somut neticelerle kuvvetlendirmeyi sürdürdük" diyen Fidan, ASEAN ile Diyalog Ortağı ilişkisi tesis eden 12. ülke olunduğunu söyledi.
Latin Amerika ve Karayipler ile ilişkilerin her alanda geliştirilmesine ve derinleştirilmesine devam edildiğini aktaran Fidan, şunları paylaştı:
"İberAmerika Konferansı'nın 4-5 Kasım'daki Zirvesi'ne ilk kez Ortak Gözlemci statüsünde iştirak ettik. Bölgemizde güvenlik ve refahı, küresel ölçekte istikrar ve barışı tesis etmek üzere yürüttüğümüz dış politikamızda Yüce Meclisimizden güç alıyor, değerli milletvekillerimizin katkılarını şükranla karşılıyoruz. Parlamenter diplomasinin dış politikamızın öncelik ve hedeflerini hayata geçirmemizde bizlere son derece değerli katkılar sağladığını ifade etmek isterim. Aynı zamanda, farklı görüş ve bakış açılarının temsil edildiği Meclisimiz, dış politikamızın hem planlanması hem uygulanması aşamalarında çalışmalarımızı zenginleştirmektedir."
Gazze'deki soykırıma değinen Fidan, "Sadece milli iradenin tecelligahı değil, aynı zamanda milletimizin vicdanının da sesi olan Yüce Meclisimizde istisnasız bütün siyasi partiler Gazze'deki soykırım karşısında sessiz kalmamış, Filistinli kardeşlerimizin yanında güçlü ve kararlı bir duruş sergilemiştir." dedi.
Filistin'in yıl boyunca Türk dış politikasının öncelikli gündem maddelerinden biri olmaya devam ettiğini vurgulayan Fidan, Gazze'de soykırımın durdurulması, insani trajedinin önüne geçilmesi ve yeniden inşa faaliyetlerine başlanması amacıyla yürütülen gayretlere, Türkiye olarak öncülük edildiğinin altını çizdi, yapıcı ve etkin katkı sağlandığına dikkati çekti.
Dışişleri Bakanı Fidan, "Aynı zamanda, Batı Şeria'daki yerleşimci terörünün, Mescid-i Aksa'ya yönelik provokasyonların ve İsrail'in bütün bölgeyi tehdit eden yayılmacı politikalarının önlenmesi amacıyla bölgemizdeki ülkelerle ve uluslararası ortaklarımızla birlikte çalışmaya devam ettik, önümüzdeki yıl da bu çalışmalarımızı artırarak sürdüreceğiz. Filistin'e destek sağlanması ve İsrail'e yönelik uluslararası izolasyonun artarak devam etmesi için yürüttüğümüz çalışmaların nihai stratejik hedefi 1967 sınırları temelinde, Başkenti Doğu Kudüs olan, Bağımsız, egemen ve toprak bütünlüğünü haiz bir Filistin Devleti'nin kurulmasıdı…

I’m often asked if Dyson products are really worth the money. As WIRED’s resident vacuum tester, I’ve tried every recent Dyson vacuum —from the newest, most powerful model to the long-favored V15 Detect—and I have a lot of thoughts on which ones you should buy, and at what price. The best time to shop is during sale season, and lucky for you, Dyson's Black Friday deals have already started as of today. If you’re looking to pick up a new vacuum before your family comes over for Thanksgiving, here's the on-sale models I recommend.
Want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals , the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals , and the Best REI Holiday Sale Outdoor Deals .
If you’re going to buy a Dyson vacuum on sale, you might as well go for one of the better ones. The V16 Piston Animal is Dyson’s most powerful stick vacuum, with 315 air-watts of power, some nice quality-of-life improvements in the body design, and an option to add the Submarine 2.0 mop head. I really liked this vacuum for the design upgrades and power level, but the price tag can be hard to stomach. It’s on sale fairly regularly, and there are a few different on-sale combos: The base vacuum is $180 off, bundling it with the Submarine head is $200 off, and the option with the charging Floor Dok is also $200 off. I love the Submarine head, but while I haven’t tested the vacuum with the Floor Dok yet, it’s the accessory I want most—having your cordless vacuum fully charged whenever you want it, and somewhere to store it, is really handy.
If you want a cheaper vacuum that still comes with two cleaner heads, the older Dyson V15 Detect is also already on sale ($599) , and it's even bundled with the Car Cleaning Kit, meaning three extra attachments. The V15 was our top Dyson vacuum pick for a long time because it's more affordable than the Gen5Detect and V16, but still packs two cleaner heads (the Digital Motorbar for carpet and Fluffy Optic for hard floors) and has 240 air-watts of suction (almost 100 more than the V10 Konical and other cheaper Dyson vacuums). It's a great all-around vacuum, and this bundle option gets you great extra attachments.
The PencilVac is incredibly handy and compact , and great if you're trying to do quick pickups daily on hard floors. You won't want it if you have any kind of rug or carpet, since it's only designed for hard flooring, but I did find it incredibly easy to grab and use for constant litter trails in my house. It's incredibly lightweight and a great fit for anyone with mobility or strength concerns. If these features speak to you, this is a great time to buy, as it's already on sale.
This wet floor cleaner is often on sale for around $400, so it's not a huge surprise to see this deal ahead of Black Friday. The Dyson Clean+Wash is primarily a wet floor cleaner, but it can do dry cleans, too, and does not use a filter you inevitably need to keep clean. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck noticed no weird smells in three months of use. It's similar to the Dyson WashG1 , with a self-propelled design that makes it easy to push around the room, and it does a good job scrubbing floors clean. Keep in mind that it's not great for dry debris, since its just rolling, not sucking.
The Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai came out earlier this year and is one of my favorite robot vacuums from the brand. That's including the newer Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV I’m currently testing, which hasn't blown me away as a better investment. (It actually failed my corner test completely, which vacuums in that price range should not do.)
The Spot+Scrub Ai is much lower priced, and despite some dubious AI feature claims, it does a good job cleaning autonomously. It’s often discounted around this price, but the $400-off sale is a little better than what I saw during Prime Day.

It's not Black Friday quite yet, but I'm already on the hunt for laptop deals, and this week, they're finally getting good. I know some people will want to wait until the weekend of Black Friday to ensure they're getting the best Black Friday deals , but there's no guarantee that the discounts will stick around until then. I'll be carefully following laptop deals through Black Friday and the holiday shopping season, so make sure to come back for more hand-picked deals on some of the best laptops I've tested this year.
Want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Amazon , the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals , and the Best REI Holiday Sale Outdoor Deals .
The MacBook Neo was already cheap, so Apple hasn't been eager to give much in the way of price cuts—despite the laptop having been out for seven months. But finally, the MacBook Neo's price has dropped by $50, bringing it down to $649. That's a great deal, especially if you're looking for an affordable laptop that feels premium, with a metal chassis and quality display. The 8 GB of RAM is limiting, but if your needs aren't overly heavy, the MacBook Neo should do the trick—especially at this price.
These days, you'll be hard-pressed to find a laptop for under $1,000 that doesn't have any major compromises. That's even more uncommon for a laptop with a larger screen. But the IdeaPad Slim 5x is just that. It's a 15-inch laptop with great performance, long-lasting battery life, lots of ports, a solid trackpad, and a high-resolution OLED screen. It even comes packed to the brim with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. It's not as thin as the 15-inch MacBook Air, no, but then again, it's hundreds of dollars cheaper.
It might be well over two years old, but I still find myself recommending the Surface Laptop from 2024. The price is down to $900 right now, which is a good deal for these specs, performance, and battery life. You're limited to only the blue color option, but it's the best price I've seen on this laptop this year so far. My favorite feature will always be the 3:2 aspect ratio screen, which gives the display a taller shape for more vertical space to work with.
There is a newer version , which comes with the Snapdragon X2 Plus/Elite chips, but I've found that it's still quite expensive. The IdeaPad Slim 5x listed above is the better option if you're OK with a larger device, since it uses those next-generation Snapdragon chips (for less money). But if you're sold on the design of the Surface Laptop, this is the one to get.
With the MacBook Neo selling for $649, you might look at something like the HP OmniBook 5 with suspicion. Even on sale for $750, being $100 more than the MacBook Neo doesn't seems like a great position to be in for an entry-level Windows laptop. And while this laptop is on sale often, this is $100 cheaper than I've seen it over the past few weeks.
The HP OmniBook 5 is a special device, with its OLED display, very thin chassis, and 16 GB of RAM. It very much looks like a laptop that should cost hundreds more. Battery life is great too, thanks to the Snapdragon X chip inside. The 16 GB of RAM is still the main selling point here—if it was any less, I would recommend the XPS 13 in nearly every scenario (but it's not on sale right now). It's only real downfall is the touchpad. It feels frustratingly clumsy one to use, making precise movements difficult.

World court to issue key verdict in its first genocide ruling in more than a decade.
The top court of the United Nations is scheduled to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority in a case brought by the West African nation of The Gambia.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague is to deliver its verdict on Thursday in what will be its first judgement on the merits of a genocide case in more than a decade.
Legal experts said the ruling could bear on South Africa’s ongoing case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza, which Israel is contesting.
The Gambia accuses Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people during a 2017 military crackdown that forced hundreds of thousands to flee. Myanmar, meanwhile, claims it was responding to attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) on police posts.
Myanmar’s military began what it called clearance operations in Rakhine State in October 2016 and a far larger campaign in August 2017 after attacks on police posts by a Rohingya armed group. About 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 740,000 forced to flee to Bangladesh, the UN estimated.
UN investigators found that soldiers razed hundreds of villages, carried out mass killings and routinely raped and gang-raped Rohingya women, girls and boys. They said the sexual violence indicated genocidal intent.
The military itself has announced convictions in only two cases brought after the violence. However, in one, seven soldiers jailed for killing 10 Rohingya men and boys at Inn Din village were freed after serving less than a year of their 10-year sentences.
In 1982, long before the crackdown, Myanmar excluded the Rohingya from its 135 recognised ethnic groups, calling them immigrant Bengalis despite many families having lived in Myanmar for generations. Nearly all Rohingya have been denied citizenship since then, making them the world’s largest stateless group .
Since fighting with the military resumed in 2023, the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group, has taken most of the state. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights said in August that both forces have committed widespread and systematic abuses against the Rohingya, accusing the Arakan Army of torture, sexual violence and forced recruitment.
The UN said those abuses have driven more than 155,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh since early 2024, taking the refugee population there up to about 1.2 million.
Nearly all the refugees live in crowded camps in the Cox’s Bazar District, where they are dependent on international aid that has fallen sharply in recent years, particularly since United States President Donald Trump’s administration slashed foreign aid in 2025. Most refugees now receive smaller food rations, and many camp schools have closed. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees warned that recent arrivals often lack sufficient food, clean water and healthcare.
The Gambia said it brought the case after decades of persecution of the Rohingya that culminated in the 2017 operation, which it argued breached the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The Muslim-majority nation of 2.5 million people filed the case in November 2019 on behalf of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). The case was led by Abubacarr Tambadou, then The Gambia’s attorney general and justice minister.
In January 2020, the court ordered Myanmar to take emergency measures to prevent genocidal acts.
Myanmar initially argued that The Gambia, which was not directly involved in the conflict, could not bring the case. But in 2022, judges ruled that it could because both countries are parties to the convention, under which all signatories are obligated to prevent and punish genocide.
Hearings on the merits of the case followed in January this year with seven states – including Canada, France and the United Kingdom – backing The Gambia.
The judges must decide whether Myanmar, as a state, committed genocide against the Rohingya, thereby breaching the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.
The ICJ passes judgements on state actions. It does not rule on the criminal guilt of individual soldiers or commanders.
Under the convention, “genocide” refers to acts such as killing and causing serious harm committed with intent to destroy, wholly or partly, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
Evidence that a state has committed atrocities is not enough. The court must also find they were carried out with specific intent to destroy a group. Such intent can be shown through direct statements or orders or inferred from a pattern of conduct.
The Gambia argued that genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference from Myanmar’s conduct.
Myanmar, meanwhile, said it was conducting a legitimate counterterrorism operation against Rohingya fighters, not targeting Rohingya people as a whole.
A genocide finding would formally recognise the harm the Rohingya have suffered but may do little in the short term for the more than one million victims of violence and displacement, said Michael Becker, an international law professor at Trinity College Dublin and a former ICJ legal officer.
The Gambia wants the court to order Myanmar to ensure displaced Rohingya can return safely to their land, compensate them, and replace or rebuild destroyed homes and property.
Becker told Al Jazeera the court may impose those demands only partly or in general terms, leaving Myanmar to decide how to comply with them.
Such an outcome would “surely be disappointing” to those who are sceptical that the government would fulfil those demands in good faith, he said.
“Even if the ICJ were to order far-reaching forms of relief, the political conditions on the ground in Myanmar are not amenable to realising that relief anytime soon,” Becker said.
He said a finding would instead have to be used to pressure Myanmar diplomatically.
William Schabas, an international law professor at Middlesex University in the UK, said the measures that The Gambia was seeking on behalf of the Rohingya were “robust” even though they fell short of demanding citizenship, which would end their statelessness.
“Assuming Myanmar implements the conclusions, this will indeed have significant positive effects on the security, dignity and livelihoods of the Rohingya in Myanmar,” Schabas told Al Jazeera.
The Myanmar ruling will be the first final judgement out of five genocide cases pending before the ICJ.
Becker said the outcome could clarify the court’s longstanding “only reasonable inference” test. Under it, judges infer genocidal intent from a pattern of conduct only if no other reasonable explanation fits.
He said the court’s two rulings on the Balkan wars left it unclear whether genocide could be deemed to occur alongside armed conflict, which he said was “an unduly restrictive standard”.
Thursday’s judgement could instead treat armed conflict as an alternative explanation for a party’s conduct, rather than an automatic bar to establishing genocidal intent, he said.
According to Schabas, the ruling will “have very dramatic effects” on the outcome of the other pending cases, particularly the case against Israel.
“In my opinion, the South African case against Israel is much stronger than the case of Gambia against Myanmar. If Gambia wins against Myanmar, we can be confident that South Africa will prevail over Israel,” he said.

In case filed at the ICJ in 2019, The Gambia accused Myanmar of breaching the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The United Nations’s top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya population.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague delivered its judgement on Thursday over the military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 mainly Muslim Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.
ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention.”
It is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court. The ruling marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the crime had been committed.
The case was brought by the West African nation of The Gambia, which in 2019 accused Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people. It asked the ICJ to rule that Myanmar has breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order the nation to put an end to any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished.
Myanmar, meanwhile, has claimed its crackdown was in response to attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) on police posts.
Evidence shows Myanmar forces killed some 10,000 Rohingya, Iwasawa said during a three-hour readout of the verdict.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya ⁠civilians, perpetrated widespread acts ⁠of sexual violence as well as acts of ⁠extreme violence against children and ⁠attacked fleeing Rohingya ⁠as they sought to flee in large numbers to ‌Bangladesh,” he added.
In specific cases that he referred to, he said Myanmar had acted with “genocidal intent”.
The ICJ said that the “only reasonable inference” from evidence of widespread atrocities by Myanmar security forces is that they had the intent to destroy a “substantial part” of the Rohingya minority.
It said Myanmar should have known that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians participated in the military campaign.
“Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” it added.
The court established that at least four genocidal acts have been proven: the mass killing of civilians, the forced displacement of hundreds of thousands of people, serious harm inflicted upon this group, and also the prevention of birth, said Al Jazeera’s Step Vaesen, reporting from the Hague.
Rohingya long have been treated as second class citizens, well before 2017, according to the judge, she said. They were also forced to take part in a birth control programme, she added.
“So the judge really saw this as a very strong explanation that … a genocidal act was committed there,” said Vaesen.
“It’s extremely important for the Rohingya because they’ve been waiting for 10 years for any kind of justice, but it’s also important for the whole international community because genocide is such a difficult act to prove.”
The hardest part of any genocide case is proving specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part – an extremely high bar, said Toby Cadman, an international human rights lawyer. He noted that the ICJ had never before ruled that a state has specific intent to commit genocide.
“The court is guided by the genocide convention and what the genocide convention states and it is a high threshold,” Cadman told Al Jazeera.
He said the situation does not end with the ICJ’s ruling, and that a lot will depend on what what comes next, whether this goes before the UN Security Council, or whether there are sanctions, or other remedies that the court can order to ensure that it’s enforced.
More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in sprawling refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh, according to the UN.
Conflict, shrinking humanitarian aid and dangerous sea crossings continue to leave many members of the community displaced and vulnerable.

The United Nations International Court of Justice on Thursday ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Muslim Rohingya minority. It is the ⁠first time a state ​has been ‌found responsible for genocide at the ‌court.
The top United Nations court ruled on Thursday that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar 's security ​forces against the Rohingya ‌Muslim minority population in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide .
The decision, seven years after the ⁠case was filed by predominantly Muslim Gambia, marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the legal threshold to prove genocide ‌had been met. It was the first time the court held a state responsible for genocide .
"The ⁠court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya," presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa said ​in a reading of the decision.
Read more 'Targeted for destruction': Top UN court hears Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
The panel found "that the Republic of the Union of ‌Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine State".
Judges found that Myanmar's military carried out mass executions of men and boys, committed widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women and burned or razed hundreds of villages during so-called clearance operations. ‌The military actively spread hate speech targeting the Rohingya population, they said.
Myanmar's military offensive drove at least 700,000 Muslim Rohingya from Buddhist-majority Myanmar.
A panel of 15 judges said "the ​only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group namely the Rohingya population in Northern Rakhine state", meeting the legal threshold for genocide.
For the more than one million Rohingya now living in the world's largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh , the historic ruling offers a glimmer of hope for accountability.
"I want justice ," a 23-year-old Rohingya rape survivor said in the cramped shelter where she lives with her family.
"There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women. The ICJ should say something separately about this," she said, requesting anonymity.
Survivors of the violence brought with them harrowing tales of gang rapes, mass executions, and cruelty towards families and children.
Far from the squalor of the refugee camps, the panel of 15 judges has been weighing for seven years whether Myanmar's actions constitute genocide.
The case was brought by the Gambia under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to bring a case against another it suspects of breaching the international agreement set up after World War II .
While the ICJ has no way of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing .
He commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.
This year he was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy which may be complicated by the ruling.
Myanmar has always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.
"Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein," its representative Ko Ko Hlaing told judges during hearings on the case in January.
The Gambia 's justice minister said the country filed the case "after reviewing credible reports of the most brutal and vicious violence imaginable inflicted upon a vulnerable group that had been dehumanised and persecuted for many years".
The Gambia has the "full backing and support" of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation for its efforts at the ICJ, said the minister, Dawda Jallow.
"It is not about esoteric issues of international law, it is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings," added Jallow.
"The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction."
Genocide is notoriously difficult to prove in international law because the Convention requires proof of a specific "intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group".
The Gambia argued during the hearings that genocidal intent was clear from the "organised nature and execution" of the crackdown, its "extreme brutality", the "pervasive sexual violence", and the targeting of children.
Legal experts are watching the case closely for clues as to how the ICJ will handle another seminal case before it – accusations by South Africa that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Survivor Mohammed Osman said he was hoping the verdict would allow him to go back home and perform last rites for his parents and younger brother killed by the Myanmar military.
"They shot my father dead, forced my mother into a house with a few other women, raped them and burnt down our homestead," Osman, 20, told AFP.

The three leaders have divergent geopolitical goals and visions for the world order.
On November 19, the leaders of China, the United States and Russia will gather for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen on the sidelines of an annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. The three have never met for formal trilateral talks, and some commentators are already calling the meeting “historic”.
In Moscow, many observers see the gathering as a “new Yalta” – another conference to divide the world into spheres of influence, similar to the one held in 1945 between Britain, the USSR and the US.
This thinking reflects Russian President Vladimir Putin’s own worldview. It is perhaps unsurprising that he was the one to propose the trilateral meeting during a call with US President Donald Trump in October.
A “new Yalta”, however, appears to be more of a case of wishful thinking than a realistic possibility. In 1945, the Soviet Union, the US and Britain came together after emerging victorious from the second world war, in which they fought against a common enemy. Today, not only do they find themselves on opposing sides of various conflicts and disputes, but they also seem to disagree on how the world should run.
While all three powers speak of a new, multipolar world and formally reject the language of hegemony, they seem to have divergent understandings of what that means.
Moscow, for example, seeks to establish itself as one of the poles in a multipolar world and a regional leader in Eurasia.
Washington, on the other hand, wants to secure its status as the pre-eminent power, while Beijing remains preoccupied with pulling the Global South away from US leadership.
Therefore, the US and China are championing a bipolar system – a world shaped by the “G2” as Trump calls it – which Russia might be unhappy with but has no means of stopping.
This disparity of aspirations is also apparent at the economic level. While Russia has chosen a path towards archaisation and opposes almost any manifestations of progress, the US and China are leading the world in technological innovation and competing in spheres such as semiconductor production, mobile communications, space exploration, robotics, biotechnology and, most recently, artificial intelligence (AI). In all these spheres, Russia has fallen behind not years, but decades.
These divergent visions are reflected in the apparent disagreement over what this summit should be about.
Trump has said he would prefer to address nuclear disarmament, a topic that is unpopular in China given that it has the smallest nuclear arsenal of the three countries. Russia, too, is not very eager given that it is relying on its nuclear arsenal as the last remaining element of its great-power status.
Putin, on the other hand, wanted to focus the summit on the settlement of the Ukraine war without the Ukrainians and Europeans present. Yet, it is unclear what can be achieved in a sit-down with Trump and Xi Jinping, given Putin’s maximalist demands.
As the recent consultations in Abu Dhabi and Moscow demonstrated, the Russian president wants profound changes to the current European order that simply cannot be secured because they would be in violation of international law.
Even if a rollback of NATO might appeal to China, Putin’s insistence on violating the principle of sovereignty would be too much for Beijing. Therefore, I cannot imagine President Xi willingly engaging in discussions that are bound to face a dead end.
Instead of entertaining his guests’ unrealistic agendas, Xi is likely to yield to no more than a general declaration on cooperation and common understanding.
For him, the summit is a long-awaited – and much-deserved – foreign policy triumph, and an acknowledgement of China’s standing in the world.
After all, he will be hosting the leaders of the two states that Beijing had looked up to as superpowers for the better part of the last century. From the late 1940s, China was highly dependent on the USSR, and even after the Mao-Khrushchev break, it replicated many Soviet policies and technologies.
Then with the launch of market reforms in the late 1970s, Beijing gradually became the most talented disciple of the US-led West, masterfully convincing the Americans that its economic rise would benefit everyone while capturing global markets through formal acknowledgement of World Trade Organization (WTO) rules and intellectual property laws.
In this sense, it is highly symbolic that China welcomes the leaders of Russia and the US at a time when it dominates global manufacturing and trade, has the fastest-growing economy of the three powers, and is a frontrunner in the global technology race.
There is also quite the contrast between the level-headed Xi and his US and Russian counterparts, whose irresponsible policies have dragged their countries into disastrous wars they cannot win or get out of.
In the end, the summit may lay the foundations of a new trilateral format between China, the US and Russia. Each leader may have their own reasons to maintain it: Trump would like to continue with his unilateral policies, sidelining traditional allies; Putin desperately wants to become a part of something reminiscent of the old times when Moscow was a superpower; and Xi might use this format to institutionalise a G2+1, knowing that the +1 – Russia – will be dropped after the Ukraine war ends and the world’s attention to the Kremlin diminishes.
Yet, little of substance would come out of these meetings. These would not be venues where the pressing issues of the world would be resolved.
And in any case, Xi, Trump and Putin may not be capable of resolving them. After all, they belong to an outgoing generation of policymakers representing a world captured not so much by powerful ideologies or leadership aspirations, but rather by memories, nostalgia, old phobias and prejudices.
In the coming years, it may happen – as it did after the “old Yalta” – that they no longer occupy positions of power and a new generation will take their place, leading the world into a better future.

The unprecedented trilateral meeting in Shenzhen between US President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin ended on Thursday without statements from the three leaders, after Trump declared at the beginning that the three global powers "are making history".
Opening their first such summit, which could be a pivotal moment in world history, Trump said the three leaders “will talk about all problems that are being discussed in the world.”
“We have great responsibilities to solve problems that affect the entire planet," he added.
Trump said he had a "long discussion" with Putin on Russia's ongoing all-out war in Ukraine and that all sides "would like to see an end to that war".
Xi joined Trump in saying their summit “has groundbreaking significance”, adding that “the world is at peace when great powers live in harmony," calling on the three countries to “abandon Cold War mentality, not pursue decoupling and breaking chains”.
"The three countries should work together to address global challenges,” and that they "can strengthen coordination to safeguard global energy supply chain stability," Xi said. “Adversity reveals true responsibility.”
Putin said that Russia’s war in Ukraine would be part of the talks, stating that “we have shared interests in Ukraine.”
“Russia, the US and China are united not only by their status as victorious nations in World War II, but also by their responsibility for maintaining international peace,” Putin said.
However, after the summit ended, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the Russian media that Ukraine was not "the central topic" at the summit.
Just as the summit was starting, China's state news agency published a statement from Xi saying that “nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, building a nuclear-free world.”
In his opening statements, Trump said that the “three countries are uniquely positioned to discuss nuclear weapons."
“Too often past leaders avoided talking to leaders they had disagreements with,” Trump added.
The leaders posed for a family photo without shaking hands as they started their summit and made no statements when it concluded.
The meeting ended after around an hour and 20 minutes. Trump left the venue immediately for Shenzhen's airport and took off shortly after, while Xi accompanied Putin who also departed for Russia.
China's state news agency Xinhua published the full text of what it called the "trilateral peace declaration," listing four key points: commitment to UN reform, plans to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, respect for the immunity of state officials and opposition to the ICC and similar institutions abusing their jurisdiction, as well as an agreement to hold dialogue on nuclear risk reduction and non-proliferation.
The declaration makes no explicit reference to Ukraine, Iran, Taiwan or North Korea.
The US and Chinese presidents met bilaterally earlier on Thursday in their third substantial meeting this year.
During the meeting, Trump said that the US and China want to help end the war in Ukraine, stating that "we're looking to both help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine."
The US president praised their friendship and their shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, which has become a key site of attacks in the Iran war.
Xi said that relations between the US and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump’s presidency.
“The efforts you have made are there for all to see and will go down in history,” Xi said.
Trump also met Putin ahead of the trilateral, stating that “we’ve had a great relationship for many years.”
Their meeting marks the first time the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia's all-out war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start,” Trump said as he greeted Putin, saying "Who is he? He's my friend."
The summit has stoked fears that the three powerful men may seek to divide the globe into spheres of influence, for example by making decisions that affect Ukraine's fate over the heads of Kyiv or Europe.
A wider debate raged among observers on social media over whether the summit can be dubbed a "Yalta 2.0," while others claim it should instead be dubbed Munich 1938, given the fundamental differences in time, space and the protagonists.
To underline the summit's weight and balance European and wider Western media coverage, Asian television stations and newspapers focused on the possible consequences for their own countries.
Chinese state media, particularly Xinhua and People's Daily, framed the APEC summit and the trilateral around Xi's diplomatic leadership, multilateral cooperation and China's commitment to free trade. Beijing is presenting the trilateral summit as an opportunity to promote global peace and strategic stability among major powers.
In South Korean media, a recurring theme was concern over a potential “Yalta 2.0” conference, in which leaders could discuss the future of the Korean peninsula without Seoul's participation, with news agency Yonhap reporting that the South Korean government has conveyed these concerns to both Washington and Beijing.
The coverage is also focusing on the possibility of renewed US–North Korea dialogue and the risk of tacit acceptance of North Korea's nuclear status.
Japanese media are focusing on strained Sino-Japanese relations, with one major TV channel reporting on the first face-to-face encounter between Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Xi in about a year.
No formal bilateral meeting between Takaichi and Xi has been scheduled, and the Japanese media reported that Takaichi was seeking a discussion with Trump following the trilateral summit.
Germany was also due to host Ukraine's allies for a "Coalition of the Willing" meeting on Thursday involving US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
