US president calls both Putin and Xi a ‘friend’ in separate meetings ahead of rare three-way talks in China.
United States President Donald Trump has met with his Chinese and Russian counterparts for highly anticipated trilateral talks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ( APEC ) summit.
Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin met for a “family photo” before convening for talks on the sidelines of the summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in an unprecedented gathering of the world’s three superpowers.
Opening the meeting, Xi said that it “has groundbreaking significance”.
“The world is at peace when great powers live in harmony,” Xi said, adding that the three countries “should work together to address global challenges”.
In a major statement, the Chinese leader also said “nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, building a nuclear-free world,” reported China’s Xinhua news agency.
In Trump’s opening remarks, the US president said the three countries are “uniquely positioned” to discuss nuclear weapons.
“Too often past leaders avoided talking to leaders they had disagreements with,” he said. “No peace ever forged by declining opportunities.”
Meanwhile, in his opening remarks, Putin made it clear that the war in Ukraine would be the focus of his conversation, before the three retreated into closed-door talks which lasted for about 55 minutes.
The talks between the leaders of the world’s largest nuclear powers were not likely to produce major agreements, analysts say, given deep differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade. But the meeting had unnerved smaller countries that feared their interests might be disregarded.
Ahead of the trilateral gathering, Trump held separate bilateral meetings with both Xi and Putin on Thursday.
The US president described Xi as a “friend” and said Washington and Beijing enjoyed a “special relationship”.
“As long as the two of us are in charge, I don’t think we’ll have a problem,” Trump said in opening remarks at his meeting with the Chinese leader. He also boasted that “no other countries can do what we can”.
Trump said the US has done “amazing” things in the past two years, since he returned to power, while praising China for many of its gains over several years.
Xi, meanwhile, said that he remained committed to working with Trump to steer ties between their countries on the “correct course”.
Relations between Beijing and Washington have been stable and improving, Xi said to Trump at the start of their third one-on-one meeting this year, which lasted for about an hour.
“We have established a new definition of a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability, giving it new substance based on respect, fairness and reciprocity,” Xi said.
Ahead of the bilateral meeting, Trump said the Board of Trade that he and the Chinese president agreed to form at their Beijing summit in May has brought balance to the two countries’ relationship. He said the US and China had split their tariffs in a “fair way”.
Earlier in the day, during talks with Putin, Trump also called the Russian leader a “friend”.
“We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they’ll come out of this,” Trump told Putin.
A video published by the White House showed the two leaders shaking hands and Trump briefly whispering to Putin at the start of their meeting.
In another video posted by the White House Rapid Response X account, Trump was shown pointing at Putin and saying, “He’s my friend.”
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said the two leaders “discussed the conflict in Ukraine and bilateral relations issues”.
“The meeting between the Russian and US leaders went well,” Ushakov said, according to Russia’s state news agency TASS, adding that Putin left the talks “in an excellent” mood.
Thursday also features the main event of the APEC summit, as representatives of the 21 Pacific Rim economies gather for discussions that will include high-stakes diplomacy, Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu said, reporting from Shenzhen.
“Xi Jinping, who spoke at the banquet last night during the opening ceremony, said the discussion will centre on promoting mutual openness, innovation-driven growth and results-oriented cooperation,” said Yu.
On the US-China-Russia talks, James Bays, Al Jazeera’s diplomatic editor, said that when it comes to Trump, “his personal role always matters to him”.
But, he added, “something worth bearing in mind: you have three leaders here, Trump, Xi, and Putin. Putin has been in power; he’s been in the main driving seat in Moscow for 26 years; Xi’s been there for 14 years; and they know President Trump only has 26 more months.”
Speaking to Fox News earlier on Thursday, Trump highlighted the pomp surrounding his arrival. Xi greeted Air Force One on the airport tarmac on Wednesday, which contrasted with the more muted greetings offered to other leaders.
“This is a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Trump said when asked what he wanted to get out of the trilateral summit.
Trump has insisted that nuclear arms control be a central topic of the meeting, despite Beijing’s repeated objections to talks on the issue with Washington and Moscow, which have far larger nuclear arsenals.

Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time
Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.
World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.
European football's governing body Uefa only identified its candidate Diallo fewer than 48 hours before Wednesday's deadline.
French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo, 63, received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee.
Japan Football Association honorary president Tashima, 68, announced his intention to stand against Infantino, 56, earlier this month.
Tashima is a member of the Fifa Council and a former international footballer and coach.
Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega had also said he intended to stand but was not named as a candidate by Fifa on Thursday.
A late and surprise choice, Diallo said: "I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win."
But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.
Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.
But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.
So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?
Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency
An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.
In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.
According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.
"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.
"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."
Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).
However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.
Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team
While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer," he admitted.
Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.
Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."
They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.
Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."
McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.
"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."
Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.
As recently as August it all seemed very different. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour strongly criticised Infantino for the FFE scheme, while a senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned. The heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - then signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".
Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered a series of setbacks.
First, Fifa's executives backed Infantino at a crunch meeting in Rabat. Uefa then called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, while potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stay for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.
Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by £2.6 billion.
Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.
"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.
"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.
"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."
"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."
So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?
Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.
The legal action has not yet appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

texts.https://www.theguardian.com/football/202:
Fifa has confirmed that Gianni Infantino will face challenges from Philippe Diallo of France and Japan’s Kozo Tashima in March’s presidential election.
The president of the French Football Federation and honorary president of the Japan Football Association submitted nomination letters with endorsements from five member associations by Wednesday night’s midnight CET deadline. The former Switzerland and Tottenham defender Ramon Vega has not met that threshold, despite repeatedly saying he would stand.
“The candidatures have been forwarded to the electoral committee for examination and for passing a decision on the admission of the candidate,” Fifa said.
The election in Rabat on 18 March will be the first time Infantino has faced opposition since he was first elected in 2016, when he defeated the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88.
Infantino had been expected to be re-elected unopposed for a third time after declaring his candidacy in April and had received more than 200 letters of endorsement from national associations by the time of last summer’s World Cup, but the emergence of his Fifa Forward Enterprise plan has led to a haemorrhaging of support.
Uefa has led a campaign to unseat him since July with backing from Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, and initially the AFC, but with Infantino conducting a global tour to rally support from smaller nations they have struggled to put up an alternative candidate.
Tashima was the first to declare last month in defiance of the AFC, which after criticising the FFE proposal is backing Infantino , having come under pressure from the region’s two major financial powerhouses, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
As revealed by the Guardian on Monday, Diallo was belatedly chosen last weekend as the Uefa candidate after a complex selection process. The 63-year-old’s emergence was a surprise because Uefa had initially hoped to field a more high-profile candidate, such as Arsène Wenger. The Hungarian banker Sandor Csanyi, the president of his country’s FA, had strong backers owing to his close relationship with Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin.
Diallo and Tashima may yet join forces in an attempt to defeat Infantino amid concerns of splitting those opposed to the president among the 211 Fifa members. Were that to occur it is expected Tashima would stand aside, a development that would be supported by Uefa.
All three candidates will be vetted by Fifa’s governance, audit and compliance committee, chaired by the Infantino ally Bruno Chiomento, before the nominations are confirmed on 18 February.

Residents fled the area near Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps following the Israeli evacuation order
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.
In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.
Automatic gunfire could be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".
At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu
The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.
Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road , Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.
An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza .
The military ​has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.
A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.
Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.
Residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics said one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.
In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics said two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.
Israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it says has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.
Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.
Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.
The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.
In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.
Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its military campaign in response to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.

Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.
Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies , a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking , this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.
Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.
“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”
So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.
The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.
As the head of Internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”
Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the Internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”
In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services , for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.
In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.
On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.
It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.
Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS , Google Cloud Platform , and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products , Google Workspace , telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.
When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the Internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon —but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net . Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts .
When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off Internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.
Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what’s actually going on,” she says.
Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.
Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious Internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that …

All 109 Danish lawmakers present approved the deal, easing tensions over Trump’s desire to annex the Arctic island.
The Danish parliament ⁠has unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States covering Greenland, aimed at bolstering security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
Thursday’s decision to approve the deal signed in September eases tensions over US President Donald Trump’s desire to annex the Arctic island.
In the 179-seat parliament, known as the Folketing, the 109 members present voted in favour of the text, which was adopted without opposition or abstention.
The vote, which followed the second reading of the text, went through without any debate or opposition.
In early November, Greenland’s parliament had passed it by 16 votes, with seven abstentions.
The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September to resolve tensions after Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of ⁠the mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory home to 57,000 people.
The deal is not subject to a vote by the US Senate. The executive ‌agreement, following Thursday’s vote in Copenhagen, will enter into force once the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs informs the US in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete.
Signed in New York on September 22, the agreement supplements a 1951 accord on the US military presence in Greenland.
It allows the US to build two military bases in Greenland and blocks countries outside the European Union and NATO from strategic sectors, in order to stop China or Russia from gaining influence over the territory, particularly through investments.
Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark, but the deal is to remain in force even if Greenland gains full independence.
Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that the US needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and other partners.
The shortest route ‌from ‌Europe to North America runs via strategically located Greenland, where the northernmost US military base is located.

Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.
The Prison Service of England and Wales submitted the request. A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said "it was only right" to ask for content that was "distressing for victims" to be removed.
The disgraced comedian is in prison after being sentenced to 10-and-a-half years following his conviction for rape and three counts of sexual assault.
Google told BBC News in a statement it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".
It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."
On Sunday, Brand's wife Laura shared a video on their YouTube channel and read out a message from Brand in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."
The MoJ spokesperson added that while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".
The Prison Service of England and Wales formally requested that the video be removed on the basis that they believed it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.
The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.
The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.
The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken.
However, speaking on BBC Breakfast, housing minister Matthew Pennycook described the video as "abhorrent" and said the government remained in "close dialogue" with Google.
Jess Phillips, the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the government "doesn't have the power to enforce that this video is taken down".
"It relies on YouTube, in this instance ... to do the right thing, which is a much, much broader argument about whether Ofcom codes that are in the Online Safety Act are there actually to protect women," she said.
An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement that the current guidance was ultimately voluntary, and "any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament".
Phillips, describing Brand as an "absolute narcissist", suggested it was "very likely" that the government would look at introducing a second online safety act to address gaps in the current regulatory framework.
"Before, we haven't had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings," she said. "This is an entirely new era."
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would not immediately demand Google remove the video, if she was in power - although agreed it was concerning "if people in prison are able to use other conduits to send messages".
Badenoch told Today YouTube was a private platform, and demanding content be taken down "without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from".
"If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that. But I'm quite worried about government intervening," she added.
Brand's message has prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.
Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."
Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the case was being "urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules".
Prisoners' phone conversations are routinely recorded, but not necessarily listened to by prison authorities. If Brand is found to have breached the rules, possible repercussions could include a temporary phone ban or live monitoring of his calls.
In 2022 notorious inmate Charles Bronson reportedly had restrictions placed on his phone use after he sent Sky News an unauthorised audio message about his bid for parole.
In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.
Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against Brand, said she found the message shared by Laura Brand on the couple's Sunday Service show "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".
Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.
"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told the Today programme this week.
She is one of the women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.
The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site, and also still active is Brand's X account, where a message last appeared on 11 November.
"There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read, referring to Meta's decision to disable Brand's social media accounts on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.
"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner, before concluding: "Stay tuned."
The BBC has approached X for comment; Musk himself has criticised Brand's conviction for historical sex offences.
Children's minister Josh MacAlister told the Today programme the Meta decision provided a clear template for taking action.
"Meta's community standards prohibit accounts owned by or run on behalf of convicted sex offenders, and it's as simple as that," he said. "Google should take this down."

Ex-minister Jess Phillips admits government does not have power to compel platforms to remove distressing content
A new online safety act is likely to be needed to tackle convicted criminals such as Russell Brand using social media platforms to broadcast messages from prison, Labour MP Jess Phillips has said.
Just days after his conviction , Brand’s wife, Laura, broadcast a message from her husband to their 6.6 million YouTube subscribers, claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences for which he had been convicted by a jury. The video has had almost 850,000 views.
The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) launched an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules. Google, which owns YouTube , has rejected a UK government request, made via the Prison Service, for the video to be taken down amid warnings that it was causing distress to sexual abuse survivors.
A Google spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube partner program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.”
Phillips, a former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, admitted the government did not have the power to compel platforms to remove distressing content of this kind.
“Ofcom codes on women’s safety online are just voluntary and frankly voluntary codes to tech companies is the triumph of hope over experience,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.
“This is an entirely new era and frankly the regulations are almost certainly not in place for the government to just demand that this be taken down.”
Passed in 2023, the Online Safety Act works to protect social media users from illegal content, as well as ensuring under-18s are not exposed to content that is not age-appropriate, such as pornography. It is being introduced on a phased basis and was expanded this year by additional legislation, updating Ofcom codes of practice. It does not explicitly address the issue of prisoners using social media platforms to directly communicate with the outside world, which in light of Brand’s platform, Phillips accepts is not sufficient.
“Regulatory frameworks, changes and potentially a second online safety act is needed, because before we haven’t had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings,” she said.
Phillips said that pressure would continue to build on organisations such as Google .
“All Google do by leaving this up is show that those codes are not good enough,” she added.
“I think it [a new online safety act] is very likely and the more that these companies show that they are not putting victims at the absolute heart of their policymaking in their content within their own content schemes. If Google want less regulation they will take this down.”
Calls by voices including the victims’ commissioner for London, Andrea Simon, for action to be taken by Google were joined on Thursday morning by ministers.
“I hope they make the same decision that Meta has,” said the minister for children and families, Josh MacAlister, noting that the parent company of Facebook had disabled Brand’s social media accounts on the basis they breached standards prohibiting accounts that were “harmful to the community”.
Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, told Sky News: “It’s quite a disturbing video, actually, but abhorrent in the message it’s conveying.”
“Imagine if you’re one of the victims of Brand’s heinous crimes and you see that video. Prisoners are already banned from making statements to the media. We think this is an exceptional case where MoJ ministers have asked Google to remove this specific content and we hope they’ll do so.”
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said she was concerned if prisoners were able to use conduits in prison to send messages, but felt that Brand’s wife was a separate person and YouTube was “a private platform”.
“Immediately demanding that private platforms take down without looking at whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from,” she said.
While the Brand case has brought the issue into sharp focus, there has been concern in the past about the continued ability to retain a presence on social media of other figures such as Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, the far-right activist known as Tommy Robinson.

The assistant referee had a 60-day recovery period after being operated on
An Ecuadorian footballer has been banned for eight years for throwing a rock at an assistant referee, leaving him requiring surgery to his face.
Jhon Perlaza was playing for Club Ciudad de Yantzaza against Club Rio Aguarico FC in a third-tier match in October when the incident took place.
The stone struck assistant referee Lenin Giovanni Ojeda Nunez in the face in the 96th minute of the game, which was subsequently abandoned.
A video on social media shows Perlaza standing up in the team's dugout to throw the stone, with Nunez instantly falling to the floor and holding his face after the object hits him. He then receives medical attention.
"The assistant referee suffered serious injuries that required surgery and a 60-day recovery period," the Ecuadorian Football Federation (FEF) said.
"The disciplinary committee found the player responsible for physical aggression against a match official and suspended him for eight years from all football-related activity, until 19 October, 2034.
"In addition, the FEF will ask Fifa to extend this sanction worldwide."
The FEF also fined his club Yantzaza $2,000 (£1,521) and ordered them to pay Nunez's medical fees of $4,369 (£3,323).
In a statement released on 20 October, three days after the match, Yantzaza apologised to the refereeing team and the fans, and confirmed Perlaza had been sacked as a result of the incident.
"As an institution, we categorically reject all acts of aggression, whether verbal or physical, both inside and outside sporting venues. We firmly believe that football should be a space of respect, coexistence, and fair play," they said.
"Once the person responsible for this regrettable incident was identified, the institution made the decision to remove him immediately, and he is therefore no longer part of our club."

The International Court of Justice has upheld large parts of a genocide case against Myanmar linked to the 2017 conflict with its Rohingya minority. It called for it to pay reparations and let refugees return safely.
The International Court of Justice on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide.
The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state.
The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.
"On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.
He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees, and to take measures to investigate and if necessary prosecute individual wrongdoing by its nationals and security forces.
The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predomiantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.
A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp .
The Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.
Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.
Aung San Suu Kyi , who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The ICJ said that by its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.
Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa said.
"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa also said that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But he also said that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and if anything fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.
At one point reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested."
He said this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.

Final moments before stretch of Crimean Bridge collapsed after Ukrainian attack earlier this week
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, Russia has said.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said that rail traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.
On Tuesday, Ukrainian missiles and drones destroyed the central road section of the critical bridge, collapsing part of it into the water.
The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.
A screengrab of the damaged Crimean bridge in the Kerch Strait on 17 November
It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China .
Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram.
Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge.
"As a result of a nighttime drone attack, train services on the railway section of the Crimean Bridge have been temporarily suspended," the ministry said in a statement on Telegram.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.
At least four people were killed in a Russian drone attack on the southern city of Odesa on Wednesday, according to Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".
President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.
That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.
Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.
Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

Assessment of damage under way, days after two attacks that destroyed road section of key bridge across Kerch strait linking annexed peninsula to Russia
The remaining Kerch rail bridge connecting Crimea to Russia was attacked overnight, leading to a halt in train services, two days after a dramatic Ukrainian air raid had knocked out the road bridge alongside.
Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea , said on Wednesday night that there had been another attack on the bridge, then added on Thursday that trains would start crossing from “approximately 4pm”.
Emergency repair workers had made “heroic efforts” to restore the track, the governor said. Nobody was reported wounded as a result of the incident, Russia’s transport ministry added.
The latest air raid took place hours before the unprecedented three-way summit in Shenzhen, China, between Donald Trump, the US president, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, his Russian and Chinese counterparts.
It was the third time that the $3.6bn bridge, built by Russia after its occupation of Crimea, has been struck in a week. On Tuesday, a 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed after a complex missile and drone attack that had been prepared and planned over several weeks.
Ukrainian military sources had indicated the timing of the attack on the road bridge was deliberate, ahead of the summit, suggesting that the follow-up raid on the rail bridge overnight may have been intended to bring it down as well.
One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said this week’s attacks were designed to embarrass Putin on the world stage. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.
For Ukraine, the bridge across the Kerch strait is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried twice to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
Earlier, Ukraine critically damaged the road section of the bridge in what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation . A span of the bridge’s road section collapsed, but the railway line was still standing.
Zelesnkyy described the earlier attack as the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, largely involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles.
Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles and Palianytsia drones struck the central road section of the bridge, bringing down its supporting arch. A range of weapons, including Ukraine’s Neputune cruise missile and the Ruta, made by Dutch company Destinus, targeted the adjacent rail section, Zelenskyy said.

North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex, the head of the UN nuclear watchdog said, in yet another sign that Pyongyang is delivering on its vow to bolster its nuclear weapons programme.
The assessment by International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi came as US President Donald Trump expressed his eagerness to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un while he is in Asia for a summit in China.
“Since mid-September 2026, a further extension to the original Yongbyon enrichment facility has been under construction with the new extension externally complete by late-October 2026,” Grossi said in a statement to the IAEA’s board of governors.
“The ongoing expansion of the DPRK’s uranium enrichment program remains a cause for serious concern.”
DPRK stands for Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.
The IAEA has not had access to Yongbyon or other locations in North Korea since the country kicked out the agency’s inspectors in 2009.
The IAEA has said it uses satellite imagery and open source information to monitor developments in the North’s nuclear programme.
North Korea has called its Yongbyon complex “the heart” of its nuclear programme.
Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon.
Observers say North Korea has taken steps to build additional uranium enrichment facilities at Yongbyon and elsewhere since Kim’s earlier high-stakes nuclear diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019.
Last year, South Korea’s Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.
While Trump expressed interest in meeting with Kim, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said no meeting was yet scheduled for Trump’s visit to China but said the president is prepared to begin a new dialogue with Pyongyang.
Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the US drops its “hostile policy” against his country and respects what he calls the North’s status as a nuclear state.
Experts say North Korea is eager to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that it could demand the lifting of UN economic sanctions.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has now arrived in Berlin for today’s meeting of the Coalition of the Willing.
“ More than 40 partners will be represented, including the team of the American President. Ukraine’s priorities are strengthening our air defence, energy and financial support, the diplomatic track, and the next steps toward ending the war and guaranteeing security,” he said.
Zelenskyy added Ukraine was “doing everything to ensure Europe’s full participation in the negotiation process and to make these meetings productive.”
“Bilateral meetings with European partners are also planned, and, of course, with chancellor Friedrich Merz. There will also be a format involving the American side and European national security advisers.”
Meanwhile, we are getting some lines from Russia’s Vladimir Putin after his meeting with Trump and Xi earlier today.
Putin said “Ukraine and Europe are not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict,” according to Reuters and Russian news agency Ria.
He also defended Russia’s “legitimate” demands on European security, Tass reported.
First leaders are starting to arrive in Berlin, and the US peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, just got out of their car.
They are expected to brief other leaders on the Shenhzen talks between Trump, Xi and Putin, among others.
Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen has said Europe “must never accept” Putin’s demands about “European security on Russian terms,” as she urged fellow leaders to “put Ukraine in the strongest possible position.”
In a statement ahead of today’s Berlin talks, Frederiksen said :
“ Putin’s demands are about much more than Ukraine. They are about European security on Russian terms. We must never accept that. That is why we must put Ukraine in the strongest possible position – both at the front and in the negotiating room.
We must strengthen Ukraine’s air defences so that they can withstand the brutal Russian attacks.
Russia is terrorising the Ukrainian population and is targeting their heat, water and electricity. Ukraine needs us in Europe to get through the winter. ”
The European Commission’s foreign affairs spokesperson Christian Wigand responded in very general terms to the trilateral meeting in China.
Speaking at the European Commission’s midday briefing, he said:
“We will continue following reports coming out of the discussions; we’ve also seen the statement that was published just a few minutes ago, so I would at this stage not go into any details here.”
Asked about Trump’s “he’s my friend” comment on Putin, the Commission’ chief spokesperson Paula Pinho said “in general, we do not comment on friendships.”
“ Russia, under Vladimir Putin’s command, is continuing its relentless attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine, and we would support all efforts, of course, to end this.”
France’s foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot had little time for Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin, telling French media that he did not expect anything important to come out of that meeting.
“These three leaders fundamentally disagree on everything, so they cannot agree on anything,” Barrot told French broadcaster RTL, quoted by AP.
“And as for this photograph that has generated so much discussion, it isn’t quite a photograph of the world’s three greatest powers, because the world’s three greatest powers are the United States, of course, China and the European Union. ”
“These three countries are meeting because they have something in common: They all border the Pacific,” Barrot said. He added: “These three leaders agree on nothing, so, in a sense, nothing is going to come out of this meeting.”
For what it’s worth, the China-US-Russia ‘peace declaration’ issued after their meeting, and published by Chinese state media , includes absolutely no mention of Ukraine or Europe whatsoever.
There is only one, rather generic, line that could be seen as close to these issues:
“The three heads of state exchanged in-depth views on the current international situation and pledged to maintain strategic stability and international security.”
The document also includes a commitment to promote UN reform, increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, as well as the leaders’ criticism of the international criminal court and declaration of intent to work on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.

Sweden’s Jessica Rosencrantz stressed it is “up to the citizens of the UK to decide how close you want to work with the EU.”
But, again, asked if Britain could rejoin the bloc and keep its historical opt-outs and rebates, she dismissed it as “a highly speculative question.”
“Let’s remember how the discussion was at the time of Brexit. In that light, I think it is amazing that we now can have a big summit together, with discussions on how we can come closer together when it comes to trade and mobility,” she said.
Poland’s EU minister Ignacy Niemczycki said Warsaw’s approach “has always been very pragmatic,” as he stressed that te EU after Brexit is “weaker.”
“I would like us, wherever possible, to work out such mechanisms so it works for both of us. … This is a country that thinks similarly to us in Europe on many issues and there is no reason for us to treat each other like enemies. We are friends and let’s find the right formula for that.
“I would encourage everyone to think seriously about the benefits of being in the EU, … and I think the people of the UK see it [too], now that they are outside the union.”
Meanwhile, foreign ministers arriving for the EU foreign affairs council meeting in Brussels are heroically trying to avoid saying anything remotely interesting or controversial in response to reporters’ questions on Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin.
Clearly, they would prefer to leave the talking to their bosses who are expected in Berlin later today.
And so, Spanish EU minister Fernando Sampedro merely said that Spain and the EU remained “strongly committed” to supporting Ukraine .
Asked specifically about his views on Trump’s comments on “his friend” Putin, he only sheepishly smiled and once again repeated his previous lines.
Sweden’s EU minister Jessica Rosencrantz said that “we don’t really know the details of this meeting, neither the agenda nor the specific issues" the leaders were planning to discuss.
“But the general principle is there should be no talks about European security without Europe; there should be no talks about Ukraine without Ukraine. That is our general attitude when it comes to issues about European security or Ukrainian security,” she said.
(For what it’s worth, her boss, Sweden’s foreign minister Maria Malmer Stenergard , was a bit more outspoken when she said early this morning that it was “worrying if we have great powers who think they should decide how the world should be governed.”)
Ireland’s EU minister Thomas Byrne struck a similar note to his Swedish counterpart, saying “nothing will be decided about Europe without Europe.”
“The only way peace can work is if Russia decides to stop its invasion.”

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis says it has intercepted missiles fired towards Riyadh and Saudi Arabia’s southern region after a loud boom was heard in ⁠the capital.
The attacks on Thursday are the latest in weeks of strikes by the Yemeni armed group targeting Saudi military, civilian and oil infrastructure.

A skyscraper in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh was damaged on Thursday after the Gulf country reported new attacks by Yemen's Houthis. Witnesses said the city's Public Investment Fund Tower, which showcases Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions, was "damaged across several floors, with windows blown out".
A skyscraper in Riyadh housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia 's sovereign wealth fund was damaged on Thursday, witnesses said, as the kingdom reported new attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited over the summer in neighbouring Yemen's civil war , where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.
In the early hours of Thursday, AFP journalists in the Saudi capital reported a powerful blast had been heard.
Around the same time, civil defence authorities issued a warning for "potential danger" but said minutes later that the danger had passed.
Read more Yemen: Why the Houthis may besiege Aden rather than storm it
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had "addressed a missile threat launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh".
"Initial assessment indicates the impact of debris, with material damage currently being surveyed," said coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki.
Witnesses later told AFP that Riyadh's Public Investment Fund Tower, which at 80 storeys, is the tallest in the city's financial district, had been damaged.
"The facade is damaged across several floors, with windows blown out," said one source who requested anonymity. Two other sources confirmed the damage.
Standing 385 metres high, the tower dominates King Abdullah Financial District, which acts as a showcase for Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions.
Read more Yemen's Houthis advance on Aden as government forces retreat to defend their capital
With imposing skyscrapers, luxury shops and green spaces, the district also hosts the headquarters of the Saudi stock exchange along with multinationals such as Goldman Sachs.
Chaired by Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the sovereign wealth fund is one of the largest in the world with more than $900 billion in assets under management.
It is also one of the main instruments for diversifying the kingdom's economy away from oil, plans which have been threatened by the latest fighting.
Malki also said Thursday that the coalition had intercepted five ballistic missiles launched towards Saudi Arabia's southern region, which borders Yemen.
The Iran-backed Houthis have stepped up their attacks against Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, striking targets including airports, energy infrastructure, military sites and Riyadh's financial district.
In October, a deadly attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 14 people and injured hundreds, forcing the suspension of flights for two weeks.
In response, the Saudi coalition has been striking Houthi targets in areas of Yemen held by the group.
On Thursday, Houthi media outlets reported that Saudi Arabia had launched another attack on Yemen's capital Sanaa.
The Almasirah television channel said Saudi forces have "once again targeted the shoe and textile factory of the Alyateem Development Foundation", citing its correspondent in Sanaa.
The Saudi coalition said it had "destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Dhamar", a city about 100 kilometres (60 miles) south of Sanaa that was used by the Houthis to strike Riyadh.

NBA’de Houston Rockets forması giyen milli basketbolcu Alperen Şengün (24), Indiana Pacers deplasmanında ikinci çeyrekte iki gözüne darbe alarak maçı terk etti. Rockets, Şengün’ün sahadan ayrıldığı karşılaşmayı 119-104 kazandı; teknik direktör Ime Udoka sağ gözde şişlik, sol gözün korneasında ise çizik olduğunu açıkladı.
Indianapolis’te oynanan maçın ikinci çeyreğinde ribaund mücadelesi sırasında Pacers oyuncusu Aaron Nesmith’in kolu Şengün’ün yüzüne çarptı. Hakemler pozisyonu inceledi ve olayı normal faul olarak değerlendirdi. Milli basketbolcu kısa süre sonra sahadan ayrıldı ve takımının devre arasına 62-46 önde girdiği karşılaşmada bir daha forma giymedi.
Rockets, Şengün’ün gece boyunca oyuna dönmeyeceğini duyurdu. Maçın ardından konuşan Ime Udoka’ya göre sağ gözde şişlik, sol gözde ise kornea üzerinde çizik var. Udoka, bunun zaman açısından ne anlama geldiğinden emin olmadıklarını ifade etti.
Şengün sahada geçirdiği 14 dakika 10 saniyede 7 sayı, 7 ribaund ve 1 asist kaydetti. Houston’da Kevin Durant 21 sayı attı; Pacers cephesinde ise Pascal Siakam 24 sayıyla maçın en skorer ismi oldu.
Devre arasındaki 16 sayılık fark, yıldız oyuncusunu kaybeden Rockets’ın ikinci yarıdaki performansıyla final skorunda 15 sayıya indi, ancak galibiyet hiç tehlikeye girmedi.
Rockets’ın bir sonraki maçı Cuma günü (20 Kasım) Denver Nuggets’a karşı. Takım, Şengün’ün dönüşü için henüz bir tarih vermedi.
Yahoo Sports’ta yer alan değerlendirmede fizyoterapist Dr. Ribu Thomas, sol gözdeki sakatlığın küçük bir çizik ya da geçici tahriş olabileceğini, bu tür basit sıyrıkların genellikle 1-2 gün içinde iyileştiğini belirtti ve Şengün’ün Denver maçında oynayabileceğini tahmin etti. Daha büyük bir kornea sıyrığı çıkması halinde ise sürecin uzayabileceğini de kaydetti.
Milli basketbolcunun durumunun Cuma günü yayımlanacak sakatlık raporuyla netleşmesi bekleniyor.

Denmark's parliament on Thursday ratified a security deal involving Greenland and the United States. The vote comes months after the US, Denmark and Greenland ​signed the ‌agreement to end a standoff with the Trump administration over the Arctic island's future.
Denmark 's parliament on Thursday unanimously ratified ​a security agreement with US President Donald Trump covering Greenland , hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island's future that has rattled transatlantic relations.
The US, Denmark and Greenland ​signed the ‌agreement in September to resolve tensions after Trump repeatedly ⁠threatened to take control of the mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory that is home to 57,000 people.
Read more US, Denmark and Greenland sign security deal to bolster Arctic security
The deal ‌was backed by 109 Danish lawmakers and none voted against, the parliamentary ⁠tally showed.
The executive agreement will, following Thursday's vote in Copenhagen, enter into ​force once the Danish foreign ministry informs the US in ‌a diplomatic note that procedures are complete.
The deal expands the US military 's role in Greenland, including permission to establish a "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right ‌to self-determination.
Trump's refusal to rule out military or economic force to acquire the island triggered a diplomatic crisis ​within NATO in January and forced Denmark and Greenland into months of intensive negotiations.
Last week, it passed a first reading ​in Denmark's parliament with backing from all parties, and lawmakers expressed relief and hope ​that the deal will normalise the situation in Greenland.
"However, ​there are many indications that this is not an end, but rather a beginning," said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, ​a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen.
"With the treaty in hand, the US will be able to demand greater influence on decisions that have security policy implications and on part of the extraction of strategic resources," he said. Other experts say ⁠the new agreement does not add much US military access to Greenland.
The shortest route from Europe ⁠to North America ​runs via strategically located Greenland, where the northernmost US military base is already located.

Habertürk 'ten Nazif Şahin Karpuz'un haberine göre; 'Aşk Tesadüfleri Sever 3'ün galasında objektiflere yansıyan Ayça Varlıer, özel hayatına ilişkin açıklamalarda bulundu.
6 yıldır aşk yaşadığı DJ Serhan Aydemir ile birlikteliğinin sona erdiğini söyleyen Varlıer, ayrılık kararını karşılıklı aldıklarını belirtti.
"Çok medeni bir şekilde ayrıldık" diyen Varlıer, "Birbirimizin arasında çok güzel bir sevgi bağı var. Ortaklaşa karar verdik, bu ilişkiyi birlikte sonlandırdık. İkimiz için de kendi yolumuza devam etmeye karar verdik. O da mutlu olacak, ben de mutlu olacağım. Çok medeni bir şekilde ayrıldık. O yüzden ben şu an işlerime güçlerime, her zaman olduğu gibi yeni projelere odaklanmaya devam ediyorum" ifadelerini kullandı.
"Aşklar, sevgiler neden biter?" sorusuna da yanıt veren Varlıer, "Her şeyin galiba bir süresi olabiliyor. Bazı frekanslar bazen tutmayıveriyor. İnsanlar kendi içlerinde evrimleşiyor, büyüyor. Hepimiz bir gün önceki biz değiliz. Bazen ilişkiler de aynı paralellikte gitmeyebiliyor. Bu demek değildir ki karşıdaki insan kötü bir insan. O titreşimler, frekanslar uyuşmadığı zaman da bu tip ayrılıklara yol açabiliyor. Ama dediğim gibi gayet iyiyiz ikimiz de. Evet, bu ilişkinin süresi bitti" dedi.
"Aşkta önemli olan emek ve saygı" diyen ünlü isim, tesadüflere inanıp inanmadığı sorusuna ise "Aşk tesadüfleri sever mi sevmez mi bu akşam filmde göreceğiz. Bakalım üçüncüsü bu. Tesadüflere inanıyorum aşkta ama aşkta önemli olan tesadüf değil; birbirine karşı olan emek, saygı gibi kavramlar bence" yanıtını verdi.

ÖSYM, 25 Ekim 'de uygulanan 2026-KPSS Ortaöğretim sınavının sonuçlarını 19 Kasım Perşembe günü adayların erişimine açtı. Sınava 2 milyon 985 bin 438 kişi başvurmuştu. Sonuçlar T.C. kimlik numarası ve aday şifresiyle ÖSYM'nin sonuç sayfasından öğrenilebiliyor.
Adaylar aylardır bu günü bekliyordu. 25 Ekim Pazar günü saat 10.15'te başlayan oturumda 120 soru soruldu; genel yetenek ve genel kültür sorularını yanıtlamak için adaylara 130 dakika verildi. Başvuranların 1 milyon 448 bin 945'i kadın, 1 milyon 536 bin 493'ü erkekti. Engelli aday sayısı 11 bin 984 olarak kaydedildi.
ÖSYM'nin internet sitesindeki duyuruya göre sınavın değerlendirme süreci tamamlandı ve sonuçlar 19 Kasım Perşembe günü itibarıyla açıklandı. Sınava lise mezunlarının yanı sıra, iki yıllık geçerlilik süresi içinde mezun olabilecek adaylar da girebiliyordu.
Sonuçlara ÖSYM'nin sonuç sayfasından T.C. kimlik numarası ve aday şifresiyle ulaşılıyor. Sorgulama için sonuc.osym.gov.tr adresine girip T.C. kimlik numaranızı ve aday şifrenizi yazmanız yeterli. Ardından puanlarınız ve sonuç belgeniz ekrana geliyor. Sonuç sayfasının doğrudan bağlantısı sonuc.osym.gov.tr/Sorgu.aspx?SonucID=10413 olarak paylaşıldı.
Bir başka yol da e-Devlet üzerinden ÖSYM Aday İşlemleri Sistemi'ne (AİS) girmek. Burada 'AİS Sınav Sonuçları' bölümünden KPSS'yi seçip sonucunuza bakabiliyorsunuz. Şifresini unutan ya da hiç almamış adayların önce AİS üzerinden şifre işlemlerini halletmesi gerekiyor.
Rakamlar sınavın ölçeğini gösteriyor. ÖSYM verilerine göre sınav gününde 415 bin 502 sınav görevlisi, 32 bin 806 güvenlik personeli ve 578 ÖSYM temsilcisi görev aldı. Binalara giriş saat 10.00'da kapandı, oturum 12.25'te sona erdi.
Sınav öncesinde ÖSYM Başkanı Prof. Dr. Bayram Ali Ersoy adayları geçerli kimlik ve sınav giriş belgesiyle erken gelmeye, sınav çevresinde gürültü yapmamaya çağırmıştı. Özel gereksinimi olduğu için ek süre onaylanan adaylara 30 dakika ilave süre tanındı.
Sonuçlar açıklandığı tarihten itibaren iki yıl geçerli. Bu süre içinde yayımlanacak merkezi ve açıktan kamu personeli alım ilanlarına bu puanla başvuru yapılabilecek.
Bundan sonraki adım ilanları ve tercih takvimini izlemek. ÖSYM'nin ve kurumların duyuruları geldikçe başvuru koşulları netleşecek; puanını öğrenen adaylar için asıl yarış bundan sonra başlıyor.
